headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers: the Lyme disease paper and the Long COVID paper, and does not describe either condition in general.

Both papers show that official counting methods (insurance claims coding for Lyme disease, diagnostic coding for Long COVID) produce lower or different counts in the setting studied compared with patient-registry or phenotyping-based identification.

The Lyme disease paper reports detailed patient-reported figures on diagnostic delay, access barriers, work loss, and healthcare utilization, while the Long COVID paper reports detailed prevalence and chronicity figures but states it has no cost, income-loss, or utilization figures of its own.

comparison_rows.dimension: Diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis before diagnosis

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 32 percentage point gap in prior misdiagnosis between persistent Lyme disease patients and acute Lyme disease patients, and that patients diagnosed late (6+ months) show a 57 percentage point higher persistent-disease rate than those diagnosed early.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report a diagnostic-delay or misdiagnosis figure; its tagged categories are limited to surveillance undercount.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic delay is central to the Lyme disease paper's findings but is not measured at all in the Long COVID paper available here.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official data undercounts cases or costs

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes that the Adrion et al. 2015 claims-based $1,000,000,000/year healthcare cost estimate is drawn from insurance claims records, which by the paper's own account likely excludes an unknown share of the roughly 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients whose providers do not accept insurance.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that diagnosis-code-based surveillance (citing 4.9%-19.0% sensitivity across health systems and under 7% for broader code-based approaches) produces lower or different counts in the setting studied than its phenotyping method, which identified PASC in 16.28% of COVID-19 patients, a 9.28 percentage point surveillance gap.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers point to different mechanisms of undercounting (insurance-claims exclusion of unbilled care versus diagnostic-code insensitivity), so the underlying problem is not the same even though both involve official data falling short.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients say their physician does not accept insurance, and that about 75% of surveyed Lyme-treating clinicians do not participate in insurance networks.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states it does not quantify access barriers directly; it only notes, as a stated limitation, that patients with limited or fragmented health care engagement may be underrepresented, which could underestimate PASC prevalence.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper attaches a quantified access-barrier figure; the Long COVID paper flags the issue only as an unmeasured limitation.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper cites an externally sourced estimate of $1,000,000,000/year in U.S. healthcare costs tied to Lyme disease retreatment (Adrion et al. 2015, claims-based, payer: insurer or health system), though this is not the paper's own primary registry measurement.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no dollar cost figures of its own; it only cites, without adopting, an external claim that PASC patients generate approximately 1.5 times higher healthcare costs than matched controls, with no dollar amount or price year given.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper provides an actual dollar figure; the Long COVID paper explicitly lacks one.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 35% of persistent Lyme disease patients have an employment status of disabled, 62% of those reporting a work-schedule impact reduced their hours, and 30% quit work altogether.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report any work hours, income loss, or productivity figures; it lists this as an explicit evidence gap.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Work-loss evidence exists only on the Lyme disease side among these papers.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 72% of persistent Lyme disease patients report fair or poor health status compared with 13% of the general population (DeLong 2019 estimate).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report a patient-reported health-status or quality-of-life figure; its measures are prevalence and chronicity based on electronic health record coding.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Self-rated health burden is documented only in the Lyme disease paper among these two.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports 19.4 annual doctor visits for persistent Lyme disease patients versus 1.09 for the general population, and 3.7 annual ER visits versus 0.43.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report visit-count utilization figures; its data source is diagnostic coding and phenotyping of chronic condition presence, not visit counts.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper measures utilization intensity directly.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states it has no direct patient out-of-pocket spending or total dollar cost figures from its own registry, no lifetime cost projection, and no breakdown by age, race, disability status, or similar subgroups.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states it has no direct medical, non-medical, or indirect cost data, no COVID-negative comparator group, and no breakdown by age, race, disability status, or similar subgroups beyond region.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers independently flag the same type of missing cost and subgroup detail, which limits any attempt to compare total economic burden between the two conditions.

shared_themes.theme: Official counting systems (insurance claims for Lyme disease cost, diagnostic codes for Long COVID prevalence) produce lower or different counts in the setting studied than patient-level or phenotyping-based data.

evidence.note: The $1,000,000,000/year Adrion et al. 2015 claims-based cost estimate likely excludes an unknown share of the ~50% of persistent Lyme disease patients whose providers do not accept insurance.

Diagnosis-code-based surveillance (under 7% in broader approaches, 4.9%-19.0% sensitivity across health systems) identified far fewer cases than the paper's phenotyping method, which found PASC in 16.28% of COVID-19 patients.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers explicitly state they lack the cost and income-loss data needed to produce a total dollar burden estimate from their own primary data.

evidence.note: The paper states there is no direct patient out-of-pocket spending or total dollar cost figure from the registry itself, only visit counts and one externally cited claims-based aggregate.
The paper states no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in the document.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers describe a systemic gap between the scale of patient burden and the clinical or research infrastructure set up to recognize it.

evidence.note: The paper notes only 4% of persistent Lyme disease patients are seen by infectious disease specialists and quotes the National Academies describing underused patient registries and biobanks for this illness.

The paper describes PASC being managed under fragmented, specialty-specific diagnostic codes with no coordinating pathway linking presentations back to COVID-19 infection, rendering much of the burden invisible to population-level surveillance.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Later diagnosis is associated with markedly higher rates of persistent illness in the Lyme disease paper.

evidence.note: 20% of early-diagnosed patients versus 77% of late-diagnosed (6+ months) patients go on to develop persistent Lyme disease, a figure specific to this paper's registry population.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Insurance non-acceptance and specialist scarcity are described as concrete access barriers in the Lyme disease paper.

evidence.note: 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients report their physician does not accept insurance, and only 4% of these patients are treated by infectious disease specialists.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Phenotyping-based identification finds substantially more cases than code-based surveillance, with wide regional variation, in the Long COVID paper.

evidence.note: Regional PASC prevalence identified by phenotyping ranged from 13.64% to 22.69% across the four studied US regions, compared with a sub-7% diagnosis-code-based benchmark cited by the paper.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Among identified Long COVID cases, the large majority involve a chronic condition requiring ongoing management, suggesting an accumulating rather than resolving burden.

evidence.note: 89.31% of identified PASC patients (66,587 of 74,560) had at least one chronic condition, and cumulative PASC prevalence kept rising through mid-2024 in three of the four regions studied.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper provides direct patient out-of-pocket cost or total dollar cost figures derived from its own primary data source.

Neither paper breaks down its burden figures by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroup categories, beyond the disease-stage split (Lyme disease paper) or regional split (Long COVID paper) each already reports.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers: the Lyme disease paper, built from a patient-registry chartbook, and the Long COVID paper, built from a peer-reviewed electronic-health-record phenotyping study. Both separately describe official counting methods producing lower or different counts than their own more detailed data sources, but the mechanisms differ: the Lyme disease paper points to insurance-claims exclusion of unbilled care, while the Long COVID paper points to diagnostic-code insensitivity. The Lyme disease paper offers detailed figures on diagnostic delay, access barriers, work loss, health status, and utilization that the Long COVID paper does not report, while the Long COVID paper offers detailed prevalence and chronicity figures with regional breakdowns that the Lyme disease paper does not attempt. Both papers explicitly state they lack the cost and subgroup detail needed to produce a validated total economic burden estimate. This analysis does not establish which condition carries a greater overall burden; it only shows what each paper, on its own terms, reports.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison rests on a small, non-random sample: one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no cross-condition or unconfirmed papers available to add further evidence. It is not a controlled study, and agreement or disagreement between the two papers' findings does not validate either one; the papers were built from different source documents with different methods, populations, and time frames.

learning_cards.headline: Many Lyme patients report doctors who don't accept their insurance
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that 50 percent of persistent Lyme disease patients reported their physician does not accept insurance.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any measure of insurance acceptance or access barriers for its patients.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID clinics and payers track how often patients encounter physicians who do not accept insurance?

learning_cards.headline: Persistent Lyme patients report far more pre-diagnosis misdiagnosis than acute patients
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found a 32 percentage point gap in misdiagnosis rates between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients, with persistent-disease patients reporting more pre-Lyme misdiagnosis.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any comparison of misdiagnosis rates between different patient subgroups.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers compare misdiagnosis rates between patients with shorter and longer symptom duration?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme disease paper cites a large annual retreatment healthcare cost
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper cites an estimated 1000000000 USD/year in U.S. healthcare costs tied to Lyme disease retreatment, based on claims data.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not provide any dollar-cost estimate for Long COVID care.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers estimate the annual healthcare cost tied to prolonged or repeated treatment using claims data?

learning_cards.headline: Code-based counts may miss many actual Long COVID cases
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found phenotyping-identified prevalence exceeded code-based surveillance by 9.28 percentage points, and projected 14976200.0 individuals nationally with chronic PASC.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not compare phenotyping-based prevalence estimates to diagnostic-code surveillance rates.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers compare registry-based case identification to insurance-code surveillance to estimate a similar undercount gap?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could prompt Long COVID researchers to ask about insurance-access barriers, misdiagnosis gaps, and treatment costs, while the Long COVID paper could prompt Lyme disease researchers to ask how phenotyping-based case-finding compares to code-based surveillance; neither comparison establishes which condition's burden is larger.
